nodes.title: async/await State Machine & Continuation Internals
nodes.description: What the compiler expands an async method into (IAsyncStateMachine, AsyncTaskMethodBuilder, MoveNext), where allocations happen, capture of the continuation context, and how this affects perf and stack-trace diagnostics.
nodes.senior_signal: Senior describes the generation of IAsyncStateMachine (struct in Release, class in Debug), the role of AwaitUnsafeOnCompleted and AsyncTaskMethodBuilder; that the synchronously-completed path does not allocate (cached completed task, struct builder on the stack/in registers), while on the FIRST real yield the state machine is boxed onto the heap together with the builder; that at the await point the SynchronizationContext is captured (or TaskScheduler.Current if SyncContext==null). Knows about async void (exceptions are thrown into the SyncContext, cannot be awaited), an async method without await (runs synchronously + warning), fragmented async stack traces, and how to see <MoveNext> boxed objects in a dump. Middle treats await as magic.
nodes.example_probe: What does a simple async method with a single await over an already-completed Task expand into? When is there a heap allocation, and when does the method run without a single allocation? Why do you see <MoveNext> boxed objects in a dump, and where exactly does the state machine get boxed?

nodes.title: ConfigureAwait, SynchronizationContext & Sync-over-async Deadlocks
nodes.description: The mechanics of SynchronizationContext/TaskScheduler capture at the await point, the role of ConfigureAwait(false), and deadlocks caused by blocking waits (.Result/.Wait()) in a single-threaded context.
nodes.senior_signal: Senior distinguishes: the current SynchronizationContext is captured OR (if it is null) the current TaskScheduler; ConfigureAwait(false) affects a specific await, not the whole method; it is useless in ASP.NET Core (no SyncContext) but critical in libraries/WPF/WinForms (CA2007); knows ConfigureAwaitOptions.SuppressThrowing/ForceYielding (.NET 8). Reproduces the exact mechanism of the sync-over-async deadlock: the thread holds the context, the continuation is posted to that same busy context; explains why the same code does not hang in ASP.NET Core but steals a thread-pool thread → starvation, and why a Task.Run wrapper is a band-aid while the correct fix is async all the way.
nodes.example_probe: Code with await is invoked via .Result in WPF and hangs, but passes in ASP.NET Core and in a unit test. Explain physically what is captured for the continuation and where it is posted. What are three ways to fix it, and why are two of them band-aids?

nodes.title: ValueTask & IValueTaskSource Semantics
nodes.description: When ValueTask actually pays off, consumption invariants (a single await; must not cache/await twice/block), pooling via IValueTaskSource and PoolingAsyncValueTaskMethodBuilder.
nodes.senior_signal: Senior knows the rules: a ValueTask is consumed exactly once — must not be awaited twice/concurrently, must not call .GetAwaiter().GetResult() before completion, must not be stored in a field without .AsTask()/.Preserve(), must not be passed to WhenAll without .AsTask(). The win exists only on a hot path with frequent SYNCHRONOUS completion (buffered Stream.ReadAsync, Channel); on a guaranteed async path ValueTask is more expensive. Can talk about IValueTaskSource + ManualResetValueTaskSourceCore with token versioning (catches reuse) in Socket/Channels, and about [AsyncMethodBuilder(typeof(PoolingAsyncValueTaskMethodBuilder))]. Middle thinks 'ValueTask is always faster'.
nodes.example_probe: A cache-read method hits memory synchronously in 95% of cases — a Task→ValueTask migration. In which three scenarios will ValueTask silently return garbage or throw? How does IValueTaskSource use a token to catch repeated consumption after the backing object is reused?

nodes.title: Generic Covariance & Contravariance
nodes.description: in/out type parameters, why variance applies only to interfaces/delegates and reference types, the connection to CLR-level type safety, and array covariance as a historical hole.
nodes.senior_signal: Senior explains out=covariance (output positions only), in=contravariance (input positions only), why IList<T> is invariant (T is both read and written). Connects it to array covariance (string[] used as object[] throws ArrayTypeMismatchException on write), why variance applies only to reference types (value types have no common representation — different layout, boxing would be required), that the compiler checks positions while the CLR enforces them. Connects it to API design: IEnumerable<out T>, Func<in,out>, IComparer<in T>. Middle confuses it with inheritance of generic arguments.
nodes.example_probe: Why is IEnumerable<string> assignable to IEnumerable<object>, while List<string> to List<object> is not? Why can't IEnumerable<int>→IEnumerable<object> be made variant, and where inside .NET itself does array covariance fire a runtime exception?

nodes.title: LINQ Deferred Execution & Multiple Enumeration
nodes.description: Deferred execution, repeated materialization of the source, streaming vs buffering operators, variable capture in query closures, and perf and correctness pitfalls.
nodes.senior_signal: Senior says a query is a recipe, not data; a repeated foreach enumerates the source again (a duplicate database query, a duplicate Stream read, non-determinism with Random/DateTime.Now). Distinguishes streaming (Where/Select/Take — lazy) and buffering (OrderBy/GroupBy/Reverse — materialize the whole source before the first element). Knows about variable capture by a closure, when .ToList() is needed for CORRECTNESS (a snapshot of a mutable source) rather than perf, and the risk of hidden materialization of an IQueryable. Middle adds ToList() at random.
nodes.example_probe: An IEnumerable<T> coming from the network; the caller does .Count() and then foreach. What is wrong and how will it manifest in production? Which operators force the source to be enumerated completely before yielding the first element, and why does that change memory/latency?

nodes.title: Expression Trees & IQueryable Translation
nodes.description: How a lambda becomes an Expression<Func<...>>, how providers (EF Core) translate the tree into SQL, building trees by hand, and the cost of Expression.Compile.
nodes.senior_signal: Senior distinguishes Func<T> (a compiled delegate, in memory) and Expression<Func<T>> (an AST for the provider). Explains why a C# method inside Where on an IQueryable in EF Core 8 throws InvalidOperationException, how EF builds SQL by walking the tree, that Expression.Compile() is expensive and should be cached (the delegate, not compilation in a loop). Can build a tree by hand (ParameterExpression, Expression.Lambda/Call) for dynamic filters. Knows about logic leaking to the client when IEnumerable is used instead of IQueryable. Middle cannot tell where the code executes.
nodes.example_probe: Why does a predicate as Func<T,bool> pull the whole table into memory, while Expression<Func<T,bool>> is translated into WHERE? How do you dynamically build a tree for 'any string field contains a substring' without knowing the fields at compile time?

nodes.title: ref struct Lifetime, ref fields & Escape Analysis
nodes.description: ref struct semantics: the ban on heap allocation/boxing/async/iterator/lambdas, ref fields and scoped in .NET 7+, allows ref struct in C# 13, and the connection to GC compaction.
nodes.senior_signal: Senior lists the ref struct restrictions through a single invariant: the value must never end up on the heap (no class field, no boxing, no arrays, no generic argument before C# 13, no capture by a closure/async/iterator) — because the GC moves objects during compaction, and a managed pointer inside must remain valid only on the stack. Explains ref fields and safe-to-escape/ref-safe-to-escape analysis (.NET 7+), the role of scoped and [UnscopedRef], the allows ref struct constraint (C# 13). Middle does not know any ref struct besides Span.
nodes.example_probe: List where a ref struct is not allowed and which runtime guarantee each restriction protects. A method returns a Span from stackalloc — why will the compiler forbid it, and how does ref-escape analysis figure that out?

nodes.title: Span<T>, Memory<T> & Allocation-Free Slicing
nodes.description: Span/ReadOnlySpan for allocation-free slicing, why Span is not allowed in async (Memory<T> is needed), stackalloc and its limits, MemoryMarshal/Unsafe, span overloads in System.Text.Json.
nodes.senior_signal: Senior knows that Span<T> lives only on the stack (see ref struct), that async requires Memory<T> with .Span inside the synchronous portion, explains the unification of stack/heap/unmanaged under a single Span (ref+length), the danger of stackalloc in a loop (the stack is not released until the end of the method → StackOverflow) and the ~1KB threshold, copy-free slicing for parsing, string.Create, ArrayPool combined with Memory, Utf8Parser. Middle uses Substring and does not know the ref struct restrictions.
nodes.example_probe: Why is Span<T> not allowed in an async method while Memory<T> is? What happens with stackalloc inside a loop of 100k iterations, and how would you rewrite a CSV parser onto Span without intermediate substrings?

nodes.title: Records, Value Equality & with-Expressions
nodes.description: Generated structural equality, copy semantics of with (shallow), record class vs record struct, EqualityContract, and the pitfalls of mutable fields used in keys.
nodes.senior_signal: Senior knows that a record class generates Equals/GetHashCode/EqualityContract/PrintMembers/Deconstruct + a protected copy constructor, and that with is shallow (a nested collection is shared). EqualityContract includes the runtime type (a derived record != the base one even with equal fields). Distinguishes record struct (mutable by default, value equality without EqualityContract) and readonly record struct. Explains the danger of a mutable collection inside a record used as a HashSet key (the hashcode changes → the element is lost), and that a record is inappropriate for an entity with identity. Middle thinks a record is 'a shorter class'.
nodes.example_probe: Two records with identical fields, but one derives from the other — are they equal? What happens if you put a record with a List field into a HashSet and mutate the list, and why does a with-copy not protect you from the nested reference being shared?

nodes.title: Nullable Reference Types & Flow Analysis
nodes.description: Compile-time null annotations, flow analysis, contract attributes ([NotNullWhen], [MaybeNull], [MemberNotNull]), and the fact that NRTs are erased at runtime.
nodes.senior_signal: Senior emphasizes that NRT is a static annotation erased at runtime (JSON deserialization, reflection, EF materialization will put null into a non-nullable), so ! is tech debt. Knows the flow attributes: [NotNullWhen(true)] for TryParse, [MaybeNullWhen], [NotNullIfNotNull], [DoesNotReturn] for guards, [MemberNotNull] for Init methods. Explains generic T? without a constraint, the oblivious context during migration, and that Nullable<T> is a different runtime mechanism. Middle slaps ! on to silence the warning.
nodes.example_probe: The compiler does not trust your bool TryGet(out string? result) — which attribute removes the warning for the caller, and why? Do NRTs guarantee protection against an NRE when deserializing external JSON, and how do you handle it at the boundary?

nodes.title: Iterators (yield) & IAsyncEnumerable Streaming
nodes.description: Expansion of yield into a state machine, laziness until the first MoveNext, finally/using on early Dispose, IAsyncEnumerable, [EnumeratorCancellation], streaming, and interaction with EF Core.
nodes.senior_signal: Senior explains that yield generates an IEnumerator machine, the body does NOT execute until the first MoveNext (argument validation is moved into a non-lazily invoked wrapper), finally/using execute only when iteration runs to completion OR on a proper Dispose (foreach disposes; manual MoveNext does not). Knows [EnumeratorCancellation] and WithCancellation, .ConfigureAwait(false) on await foreach, that IAsyncEnumalble is lazy (does not buffer), the combo with Channels for fan-out, and the EF Core pitfall (an open reader/connection for the duration of the iteration, a crash on a concurrent query against the same DbContext). Middle thinks yield is 'a convenient way to return a list'.
nodes.example_probe: An iterator opens a file via using and validates an argument. When does the check run, and will the file be closed on break/.First()? Why does cancellation not reach the body of an async iterator, which attribute fixes it, and why does streaming from EF Core hold the connection open?

nodes.title: Delegates, Events & Closure Capture
nodes.description: Multicast delegates, an event vs a public delegate, memory leaks through subscriptions, variable capture by closures (by reference), and closure allocations on the hot path.
nodes.senior_signal: Senior knows about the leak: the publisher keeps the subscriber alive through the event delegate until unsubscription (the classic leak with long-lived services), and about multicast (an exception in one handler aborts the rest of the invocation list). Explains a closure as a hidden display class, capture by reference (the shared-variable bug in for before C# 5; foreach became per-iteration as of C# 5), the delegate+closure allocation on the hot path and static lambda (C# 9). Distinguishes an event vs a public Action field, the weak event pattern, and diagnosing the leak via GC roots. Middle confuses capture by value/by reference.
nodes.example_probe: Why is subscribing to a singleton's event from a transient object a leak, and how do you find it in a dump through the GC root chain? What does a lambda capture in for(int i...) versus foreach(var x...), and how has that changed between C# versions?

nodes.title: Pattern Matching, switch Expressions & Exhaustiveness
nodes.description: Modern pattern matching (type/property/relational/list patterns), switch expressions, arm ordering, exhaustiveness checking, and the connection to sealed-hierarchy design.
nodes.senior_signal: A Senior uses property/positional/relational/logical/list patterns as a replacement for if-else and visitor, understands arm evaluation order (top to bottom, important for overlaps) and unreachable arms. Knows about exhaustiveness: a switch expression without full coverage produces a warning and throws SwitchExpressionException (there is no true sum-type guarantee as in F#/Rust), hence the discipline of _ => throw for closed hierarchies. Will connect it to design: sealed hierarchies + pattern matching versus polymorphism (trade-off). A Middle writes switch only over an enum/type.
nodes.example_probe: Rewrite a nested if over two fields into a switch with property and relational patterns. Does C# guarantee that you have handled all subtypes of a sealed hierarchy, and what happens at runtime if you add a subtype and forget an arm?

nodes.title: GC Generations, Modes, Regions & DATAS
nodes.description: Generational GC, the generational hypothesis, write barriers/card tables, Workstation/Server/Background GC, Regions (.NET 7+), DATAS (.NET 8), and the impact of cgroup limits in containers.
nodes.senior_signal: A Senior explains the generational hypothesis and why gen0 is cheap, describes the write barrier + card table for gen2→gen0 references and their cost on every write to a ref field, distinguishes Background GC (concurrent mark of gen2) from the legacy Concurrent GC, understands that Server GC = a heap + thread per core (throughput at the cost of RSS and tail latency), Regions instead of segments (.NET 7+), DATAS (.NET 8, dynamic adaptation of the heap count). Critically: the impact of cgroup CPU/memory limits and GCHeapHardLimit. A Middle: 'there are three generations, gen2 is rare'.
nodes.example_probe: A service in a 2 vCPU container showed RSS growth and worse p99 after switching to Server GC. Explain it via the number of heaps, the write barrier, and long-lived objects. How does DATAS in .NET 8 change the picture, and what would you configure instead of rolling back to Workstation?

nodes.title: Large Object Heap (LOH) & Fragmentation
nodes.description: The LOH as part of gen2 for objects >=85000 bytes, sweep without compact, fragmentation as a cause of OOM with free memory available, mitigations via pooling and chunking.
nodes.senior_signal: A Senior knows the 85000-byte threshold, that the LOH is collected (sweep, not compact) only during a gen2 GC, that LOH fragmentation is a classic cause of OOM with free memory available, and proposes mitigations: ArrayPool<T>/MemoryPool, RecyclableMemoryStream, splitting into chunks <85K, preallocating capacity; understands LargeObjectHeapCompactionMode as an expensive escape hatch. Knows that LOH objects go straight to gen2. A Middle: 'large arrays are just slower'.
nodes.example_probe: A service parses 200KB JSON payloads thousands of times per second and after a day crashes with OOM at 40% free memory. Where is the LOH involved, why doesn't gen2 GC return memory to the OS, and how would you rewrite the allocations (Utf8JsonReader/ArrayPool/Pipelines) to avoid hitting the LOH?

nodes.title: Value Types, Hidden Boxing & Defensive Copies
nodes.description: Copy-by-value semantics, stack vs heap as a simplification, hidden boxing/unboxing, the default ValueType.Equals/GetHashCode, hidden defensive copies when accessing non-readonly members via readonly/in, mutable struct as an anti-pattern.
nodes.senior_signal: A Senior finds hidden boxing: a struct through an interface, a struct in an object collection, an enum in string.Format/params object[], the default ValueType.Equals/GetHashCode (reflection-based, allocating). Will explain that calling a method/property of a non-readonly struct through a readonly field/in parameter creates a hidden defensive copy (a silent perf degradation on the hot path, fixed by readonly struct/readonly members). Knows how readonly struct, in, where T:struct, IEquatable<T> eliminate these, and that 'on the stack' is a simplification (escape, class fields, closures, async — go to the heap). A Middle: 'struct is on the stack, class is on the heap' and stops there.
nodes.example_probe: In a hot loop a struct key is put into a Dictionary without overriding Equals/GetHashCode — what are the three sites of boxing/slow default comparison, as visible in a profiler? Separately: a readonly field of a large non-readonly struct, you read a property in a loop — why does the profiler show copying and how do you remove it?

nodes.title: GC Roots, Pinning, GCHandle & Pinned Object Heap
nodes.description: GC roots (stack, statics, registers, GCHandle, finalization queue), pinned objects, fixed, the Pinned Object Heap (.NET 5+), gen0/LOH fragmentation in interop, retention analysis in a dump.
nodes.senior_signal: A Senior enumerates the kinds of roots and understands how a dump finds what is keeping an object alive. Knows that the GC does not move a pinned object → long-lived pinning (a socket recv buffer) fragments the ephemeral segments/gen0, knows about the Pinned Object Heap (.NET 5+) as a mitigation and the GCHandleType values (Weak/WeakTrackResurrection/Normal/Pinned). Distinguishes GC.KeepAlive vs SuppressFinalize. A Middle doesn't think about pinning at all.
nodes.example_probe: A TCP service pins buffers for the duration of recv and suffers from increased gen0 GC and fragmentation despite ArrayPool. How does pinning interfere with compaction, how would the POH help, and how do you tell from a dump that an object is held by a strong GCHandle rather than by the stack?

nodes.title: JIT, Tiered Compilation, OSR & Dynamic PGO
nodes.description: Tiered JIT (Tier0/Tier1), on-stack replacement, inlining, devirtualization, Dynamic PGO (.NET 8 by default), ReadyToRun, and the impact on warmup and latency.
nodes.senior_signal: A Senior explains: Tier0 is fast codegen without optimizations, Tier1 recompiles hot methods based on a counter, OSR replaces the code of a long-running loop right in the stack frame, Dynamic PGO (.NET 8) collects a type profile in Tier0 and speculatively devirtualizes/inlines with a guard, ReadyToRun gives an AOT start at the cost of worse code (Tier1 catches up). Connects this to warmup, BenchmarkDotNet, and latency spikes from recompilation after a deploy. A Middle: 'the JIT compiles once'.
nodes.example_probe: A benchmark 'speeds up' by the 10000th iteration, while in production the first requests after a deploy are slow. Which phases (Tier0→Tier1, OSR, PGO) explain both pictures, and why does R2R change the 'slow start' but not eliminate recompilation?

nodes.title: Native AOT, Trimming & Reflection Constraints
nodes.description: Native AOT, IL trimming, constraints on reflection/Reflection.Emit/runtime generics, source generators as a replacement, trim/AOT-safety annotations, and the cold-start/RSS vs compatibility trade-off.
nodes.senior_signal: A Senior understands that AOT removes the JIT and Reflection.Emit/Expression.Compile, breaks string-based reflection and runtime instantiation of generics → you need source-generated JSON (JsonSerializerContext), regex, logging, DI; knows trim warnings, [DynamicallyAccessedMembers], [RequiresUnreferencedCode], [DynamicDependency] and why a library author is obligated to apply them. Weighs cold start/RSS/binary size against ecosystem compatibility and the loss of Dynamic PGO. A Middle treats AOT as 'a checkbox for speed'.
nodes.example_probe: After switching to Native AOT, a minimal API fails on DTO deserialization and on resolving a plugin via Type.GetType. Explain the root cause of each (trimming removed members / no runtime metadata) and which senior-level solutions don't boil down to 'turn off trimming'?

nodes.title: Reflection, Expression.Compile & Source Generators
nodes.description: The cost of reflection, caching MemberInfo, compiling delegates via Expression.Compile/DynamicMethod, source generators as a compile-time AOT-safe alternative, leaks via collectible assemblies.
nodes.senior_signal: A Senior knows that a reflection call is orders of magnitude more expensive than a direct one and allocates (boxing of arguments into object[]), that MemberInfo/MethodInfo must be cached, and that a hot path should be compiled once into a Func/Action via Expression.Compile/DynamicMethod, or replaced with a source generator (compile-time, zero-cost, AOT-safe). Understands that Expression.Compile is itself expensive (JIT at runtime) — cache the delegate, do not compile in a loop. Knows about leaks from uncollected dynamic code. A Middle calls GetProperty().GetValue in a loop.
nodes.example_probe: A reflection-based DTO mapper keeps CPU at 60%. What exactly should be cached (MemberInfo vs the delegate), why would a naive Expression.Compile in a loop make things worse, and why will neither approach work under Native AOT — while a source generator will?

nodes.title: Assemblies, AssemblyLoadContext & Plugin Isolation
nodes.description: Assembly loading, ALC (default/collectible), dependency resolution via Resolving, plugin unloading, type-identity conflicts ('cannot cast TypeA to TypeA'), and leaks that block unload.
nodes.senior_signal: A Senior explains the ALC model (it replaced AppDomain — no domain isolation/remoting), collectible ALCs for unloadable plugins, why any retained reference (an event handler on a long-lived object, a static, an unfinished Task, a cache) blocks unload (it happens only when there are no live references + a full GC), how Resolving and the default context resolve dependencies, and where 'cannot cast TypeA to TypeA' comes from — one assembly in two contexts = two different Types. A Middle: 'Assembly.Load just loads a dll'.
nodes.example_probe: Plugins live in a collectible ALC, but after Unload memory is not released, and a second plugin hits 'cannot cast TypeA to TypeA'. Diagnose both (what is holding the reference; where the type leaked into the default context) and how do you correctly share common interfaces between the host and a plugin?

nodes.title: Finalization, IDisposable, SafeHandle & IAsyncDisposable
nodes.description: The finalization queue, non-determinism, the Dispose pattern, SafeHandle/CriticalFinalizerObject, IAsyncDisposable, resurrection, load on the single finalizer thread under a high allocation rate.
nodes.senior_signal: A Senior knows that a finalizer extends an object's lifetime by an extra GC cycle (promotion, the finalizer thread runs ~Finalize, release happens on the next GC), that the single finalizer thread = a bottleneck under high rates, that SafeHandle/CriticalFinalizerObject are more reliable than a hand-written finalizer (execution guarantee, protection against handle recycling), when GC.SuppressFinalize is needed, and what IAsyncDisposable is for. Recognizes resurrection. A Middle writes a ~Finalizer 'just in case' and treats Dispose as a destructor.
nodes.example_probe: A dump shows a growing finalization queue and thousands of objects in gen2 with open handles. How does the finalizer delay release and why did the single finalizer thread become a bottleneck? Why does SafeHandle remove both effects, and where do you need IAsyncDisposable rather than Dispose?

nodes.title: Collections Internals & Allocation Behavior
nodes.description: Internals of Dictionary/List/HashSet, growth and reallocation of backing arrays, the role of GetHashCode/collisions, preallocating capacity, Frozen/Immutable and concurrent collections.
nodes.senior_signal: A Senior describes the bucket+entries layout of Dictionary, rehashing on growth (to a prime number, a full reallocation), the importance of GetHashCode (a bad/colliding one → chains → O(n)), the danger of a mutable key, preallocating capacity and EnsureCapacity, the tradeoff of ConcurrentDictionary (lock striping + lock-free reads) vs a dictionary under a single lock. Knows FrozenDictionary/FrozenSet (.NET 8) for read-heavy scenarios and ImmutableDictionary (structural sharing, more expensive). A Middle only knows 'O(1) amortized'.
nodes.example_probe: A Dictionary with a million entries causes latency spikes and a large LOH allocation on growth. What happens internally during rehashing, how does a bad GetHashCode turn lookup into O(n), and when would you pick FrozenDictionary over ConcurrentDictionary?

nodes.title: CLR Memory Model, volatile & Interlocked
nodes.description: The .NET memory model, reordering of reads/writes, acquire/release semantics of volatile, Volatile.Read/Write, memory barriers, Interlocked, atomicity, the difference between x86 TSO and ARM, torn reads.
nodes.senior_signal: A Senior distinguishes atomicity from visibility, understands that without synchronization a write may be invisible/visible in a different order (JIT/CPU reordering), that volatile gives acquire/release (not atomicity of 64-bit on 32-bit), distinguishes Volatile.Read/Write from a volatile field, that Interlocked operations are atomic + a full barrier, that the .NET model is stronger than ECMA (x86 is strict TSO, ARM is weaker — the bug fires on ARM/Apple Silicon). Implements lock-free code (double-check, a CAS loop via CompareExchange), knows the ABA problem, torn reads, false sharing/cache lines. A Middle thinks 'volatile = thread-safe'.
nodes.example_probe: A bool _stop flag is read in a loop by another thread and sometimes isn't seen — only on ARM. Explain this via reordering and the memory model, how volatile vs Interlocked would help, and where a torn read of a long on 32-bit fits in here?

nodes.title: Exception Handling Internals, Filters & Cost
nodes.description: Two-pass model (first pass searches for handler/filter, second pass unwinds), cost of throw, exception filters (when), throw vs throw ex, ExceptionDispatchInfo, first-chance vs unhandled, exceptions-as-control-flow.
nodes.senior_signal: Senior knows that throw is expensive (stack trace capture, two-pass: the first pass searches for catch/executes the filter WITHOUT unwinding — the original frames are visible in a dump, you can log without catching; the second pass unwinds with finally), that throw; preserves the stack while throw ex; wipes it, that ExceptionDispatchInfo.Capture/Throw carries the original stack across await/threads, why .Wait()/.Result wraps in AggregateException while await unwraps the first one. Knows about OperationCanceledException, that critical exceptions must not be swallowed, and why exceptions on the hot path kill throughput (the Try* pattern). Middle writes catch(Exception ex){throw ex;}.
nodes.example_probe: A parser throws and catches on every invalid line and is slow. Why is throw, not catch, expensive, what do two-pass and stack capture do, and how would you rewrite it (TryParse/Result)? How does throw; differ from throw ex; in a dump, and where does filter when(Log(e)) fit?

nodes.title: Middleware Pipeline & Ordering Semantics
nodes.description: The pipeline as nested closures over RequestDelegate, registration order, Use/Run/Map/UseWhen, short-circuiting, processing on the return path and HasStarted.
nodes.senior_signal: Senior will explain that the pipeline is nested closures over RequestDelegate, built in reverse order at startup; why UseRouting→UseAuthentication→UseAuthorization→UseEndpoints in that order (authz after routing so it can see endpoint metadata, but before execution), why UseExceptionHandler/UseForwardedHeaders go at the beginning. Knows that code after await next() is the return path, that writing to the response after next() is too late if HasStarted, knows about OnStarting/OnCompleted. Middle recites 'logging first, then auth' without the nesting model.
nodes.example_probe: CORS does not kick in for 401 but works for 200. Explain via nested delegates why auth short-circuits before CORS, and where to place UseCors. Why does an attempt to add a header in a late middleware throw 'response already started'?

provenance.topic: Customize ASP.NET Core behavior with middleware (HTTP logging, authentication, custom middleware)

nodes.title: DI Lifetimes & Captive Dependency Pitfalls
nodes.description: Singleton/Scoped/Transient, binding the scope to the request, captive dependency, safely obtaining Scoped from Singleton/background via IServiceScopeFactory, ValidateScopes/ValidateOnBuild.
nodes.senior_signal: Senior will explain the captive dependency: a Singleton injects a Scoped → the captured one lives as a Singleton (DbContext becomes long-lived and non-thread-safe → 'A second operation started'). Will describe ValidateScopes/ValidateOnBuild (Development), IServiceScopeFactory.CreateScope() in a hosted service, that a Transient inside a Singleton also lives forever (a Transient with IDisposable in the root scope accumulates — a leak). Distinguishes root vs scoped provider. Middle knows the definitions but does not understand why in Production it 'doesn't crash' but corrupts data.
nodes.example_probe: A Singleton needs a Scoped repository with a DbContext. In Development it throws, in Production it 'works'. What breaks under load and why is the error intermittent? Show the pattern using IServiceScopeFactory and why you must not resolve from the root IServiceProvider.

provenance.topic: Dependency injection in ASP.NET Core (built-in service container, register services)

nodes.title: Configuration, Options Pattern & Validation
nodes.description: IOptions/IOptionsSnapshot/IOptionsMonitor and their lifetimes, validation (DataAnnotations, ValidateOnStart, source-generated [OptionsValidator] .NET 8), configuration sources and precedence, hot-reload, captive snapshot in a singleton, secrets.
nodes.senior_signal: Senior will distinguish the three interfaces: IOptions<T> — Singleton, the value is fixed; IOptionsSnapshot<T> — Scoped, per-request (must not go into a Singleton — captive); IOptionsMonitor<T> — Singleton with OnChange/IChangeToken. Uses strongly typed Options instead of config["Key"] strings, validates via ValidateDataAnnotations().ValidateOnStart() (fail-fast), knows the [OptionsValidator] source generator (.NET 8, no reflection), named options, debouncing reloadOnChange, source ordering (appsettings/env/user-secrets/cmd line), the danger of secrets in appsettings. Middle injects IConfiguration and does not know why a snapshot cannot go into a singleton.
nodes.example_probe: A feature flag must be picked up without a restart, but the service reading it is a Singleton. Which interface would you take and why would IOptionsSnapshot throw an exception here? How do you make the application fail at startup on an invalid config rather than an hour later in production?

nodes.title: Generic Host & Hosted Services Lifecycle
nodes.description: IHost lifecycle, IHostedService/BackgroundService, IHostedLifecycleService (.NET 8), graceful shutdown, IHostApplicationLifetime, BackgroundServiceExceptionBehavior, cancellation via stoppingToken.
nodes.senior_signal: Senior knows that StartAsync of hosted services is sequential and blocking — long work before the first await will delay host startup. Will describe ShutdownTimeout (30s) and being cut off when exceeded, BackgroundServiceExceptionBehavior (.NET 6: an unhandled exception brings down the host by default), the StopAsync order (reverse), IHostedLifecycleService with Starting/Started/Stopping (.NET 8), Scoped via IServiceScopeFactory. Middle writes while(!token.IsCancellationRequested) without handling shutdown and exceptions.
nodes.example_probe: A BackgroundService 'dies silently' in production and queue processing halts without the application crashing. Which .NET 6 change is relevant here and how do you configure it so it crashes/restarts? Why is catch(Exception) without logging/restart an anti-pattern and how does this relate to the stoppingToken?

nodes.title: Request Lifecycle, Routing & Endpoint Resolution
nodes.description: The two-phase endpoint routing model: matching in UseRouting and execution in UseEndpoints, access to metadata between them, route precedence, MatcherPolicy.
nodes.senior_signal: Senior will explain that the endpoint is selected in UseRouting and placed into HttpContext.GetEndpoint(), while it is executed in UseEndpoints — so between them, auth/middleware reads the selected endpoint's metadata before it executes. Will describe route precedence (literals > parameters > catch-all, ambiguity), LinkGenerator vs IUrlHelper, IEndpointFilter metadata, a custom MatcherPolicy. Middle thinks of routing as a 'URL→action dictionary'.
nodes.example_probe: In a middleware BEFORE the action executes, you need to find out whether the endpoint is marked [RequiresFeature] in order to short-circuit. At what point has the endpoint already been selected, how do you get to the metadata, and why do this between UseRouting and UseEndpoints rather than duplicating routing?

nodes.title: Authentication, Authorization & Policy Pipeline
nodes.description: Separation of authn (schemes, ClaimsPrincipal) and authz (policy/requirement/handler), multiple schemes, resource-based authz, fallback/default policy, JWT validation (issuer/audience/signature/expiry, alg confusion), 401 vs 403.
nodes.senior_signal: Senior will separate authn (who — ClaimsPrincipal via schemes) and authz (what — policy/requirement/IAuthorizationHandler). Will describe multiple schemes and ForwardDefaultSelector, requirement+handler vs roles, resource-based authz (IAuthorizationService.AuthorizeAsync with a resource — cannot be done declaratively), FallbackPolicy (lock everything down), 401 Challenge vs 403 Forbid, multiple handlers for one requirement (OR via Succeed). Knows what to validate in a JWT (issuer/audience/signature/expiry/nbf/alg — alg=none/algorithm confusion, JWKS rotation), the difference between access/refresh/id tokens, why an access token must not go into localStorage (XSS), the revocation problem of stateless JWTs. Middle puts [Authorize(Roles=...)].
nodes.example_probe: A document can be edited only by its author OR an admin, and the check depends on a resource from the database. Why doesn't [Authorize(Roles)] cover this, which mechanism would you use and where would you put the logic? What does JWT validation check besides the signature, what is the algorithm-confusion attack, and how do you revoke an issued token?

nodes.title: Filters vs Middleware & Endpoint Filters
nodes.description: MVC filter pipeline (authorization/resource/action/exception/result), ordering, how it differs from middleware, IEndpointFilter in minimal APIs, access to ModelState/arguments, DI via ServiceFilter/TypeFilter.
nodes.senior_signal: Senior will explain that filters run INSIDE MVC/endpoint execution (after routing and model binding) and see action arguments/ModelState/the result — which middleware does not see. Knows the order (authorization→resource→action→exception→result), that a resource filter wraps model binding while an action filter comes after it. Will describe short-circuiting via context.Result, IFilterFactory, IEndpointFilter in minimal APIs vs MVC filters, DI via [ServiceFilter]/[TypeFilter]. Middle confuses what belongs in a filter versus in middleware.
nodes.example_probe: You need to cache an action's result and, on a cache hit, skip running model binding and the action itself. Which filter type provides this hook and why a resource filter rather than an action filter? How would you solve the same task in a minimal API via IEndpointFilter and what is the limitation?

nodes.title: Minimal APIs vs MVC: Architecture & Trade-offs
nodes.description: Comparison of minimal APIs and MVC: model binding, filters, validation, OpenAPI, performance, organization (MapGroup), AOT/source generators, model binding internals.
nodes.senior_signal: Senior will justify the choice: minimal APIs have less overhead (no controller activation, no full filter pipeline), [AsParameters], TypedResults<T> for type safety and OpenAPI metadata. Knows there is no ModelState validation out of the box — you need IEndpointFilter or the built-in validation in .NET 9 (AddValidation/source-generated), knows about RequestDelegateFactory/the source generator, friendliness to AOT/trimming (MVC's reflection gets in the way), RouteGroupBuilder (MapGroup). Will explain when MVC is justified. Middle chooses based on fashion.
nodes.example_probe: The team wants to migrate a 200-endpoint MVC API to minimal APIs for the sake of 'performance'. What (validation, filters, MapGroup, model binding, OpenAPI) will have to be rewritten, where is the real gain (AOT, no activation), and where is it just marketing for an I/O-bound API?

provenance.topic: Create a web API with ASP.NET Core controllers (RESTful CRUD operations)

nodes.title: Kestrel, Hosting Model & Connection Handling
nodes.description: Kestrel configuration (limits, timeouts, HTTP/2-3), connection model, reverse proxy/ForwardedHeaders with KnownProxies, in-process vs out-of-process behind IIS, slowloris protection.
nodes.senior_signal: Senior knows KestrelServerLimits (MaxConcurrentConnections, MaxRequestBodySize, Http2.MaxStreamsPerConnection), KeepAliveTimeout/RequestHeadersTimeout as slowloris protection, ForwardedHeaders with KnownProxies/KnownNetworks (otherwise X-Forwarded-For is ignored → https redirect and per-IP rate limiting break). Will describe in-process vs out-of-process ANCM, Kestrel as the edge in containers, HTTP/3. Middle leaves the defaults and is surprised that behind a proxy the client IP is always the load balancer's address.
nodes.example_probe: Behind nginx/ALB the application sees HTTP and the client IP equals the proxy — HttpsRedirection and per-IP rate limiting break. Which middleware and settings fix this and why are KnownProxies/KnownNetworks mandatory (what happens to security if you trust all proxies)?

nodes.title: Model Binding & Validation Internals
nodes.description: The model binding pipeline (value providers, binders, input formatters), ModelState, custom IModelBinder, [ApiController] conventions, the effect of NRT on required, why only one [FromBody].
nodes.senior_signal: Senior will explain the pipeline: value providers (route/query/form/header), that [FromBody] uses an input formatter (System.Text.Json) and only one per request (the body is a stream, read once), the rest are value-provider-based. Will describe [ApiController] (automatic 400, source inference), a custom IModelBinder/Provider, the difference between 'missing' and default, that a non-nullable reference type (.NET 6+) makes a property implicitly required. Middle knows [FromBody]/[FromQuery] but does not understand why you cannot have two [FromBody].
nodes.example_probe: Why can't you have two [FromBody], but you can have several [FromForm]/[FromQuery]? What distinguishes body binding (input formatter, stream reading) from a value provider, and how does a non-nullable string affect ModelState.IsValid without [Required]?

nodes.title: Global Error Handling, IExceptionHandler & ProblemDetails
nodes.description: UseExceptionHandler, the IExceptionHandler chain (.NET 8), IProblemDetailsService, RFC 7807, mapping exceptions to status codes, handling OperationCanceledException, stack trace leakage, exception filters vs middleware, choosing Result vs exception at boundaries.
nodes.senior_signal: Senior knows the hierarchy: UseExceptionHandler as a terminal re-executes the pipeline, the IExceptionHandler chain (.NET 8, AddExceptionHandler) gives typed handling with a bool 'handled', AddProblemDetails()/IProblemDetailsService for uniform RFC 7807 (traceId). Knows that an exception filter only catches within an MVC action (not middleware), why OperationCanceledException must not be silenced as a 500 (the client cancelled — not a server error), about stack trace leakage in Production. Distinguishes recoverable vs programmer errors, deliberately chooses Result/exception at boundaries, does not do catch+throw ex in every layer. Middle wraps everything in try/catch in the controller.
nodes.example_probe: You need uniform handling: ValidationException→400 with fields, NotFoundException→404, everything else→500 with a traceId and no stack trace, and on client cancellation — do not log it as an error. How would you build this on an IExceptionHandler chain + ProblemDetails and why won't an exception filter cover exceptions from middleware?

nodes.title: Output Caching, Response Caching & HybridCache
nodes.description: OutputCache (.NET 7+, server-side, programmable) vs ResponseCaching (HTTP headers/proxies), policies, vary-by, tags/invalidation, IMemoryCache vs IDistributedCache, cache stampede, caching of authorized content, HybridCache (.NET 9).
nodes.senior_signal: Senior will distinguish OutputCache (stores the response on the server, policy, VaryByQuery/Header/Value, tags and EvictByTagAsync) from ResponseCaching (driven by Cache-Control/Vary, not cached due to Authorization/Set-Cookie). Knows the danger of caching personalized content (leaking other users' data), vary-by-user, IMemoryCache (in-process, eviction) vs IDistributedCache (Redis, serialization), cache stampede and protection against it (single-flight/lock), HybridCache (.NET 9, built-in stampede protection and two-level cache). Middle slaps on [ResponseCache] and is surprised that nothing gets cached.
nodes.example_probe: The anonymous home page is cached server-side for 60s with tag-based invalidation on publish, while the personalized feed is never cached. Why won't ResponseCaching work (Authorization), what does OutputCache with VaryBy/EvictByTag give you, and how do you prevent a cache stampede when a key expires under load? Would HybridCache help?

nodes.title: HttpClientFactory, Handler Lifetime & Outbound Resilience
nodes.description: IHttpClientFactory, named/typed clients, HttpMessageHandler lifecycle, socket exhaustion and DNS, delegating handlers, AddStandardResilienceHandler, the danger of retrying non-idempotent requests.
nodes.senior_signal: Senior will explain two problems: (1) new HttpClient() per request → socket exhaustion (TIME_WAIT), (2) a static singleton → doesn't see DNS changes. IHttpClientFactory solves this with a pool of reusable HttpMessageHandler instances with HandlerLifetime (2 min) and rotation. Knows that a typed client is Transient but the handler is pooled, DelegatingHandler for cross-cutting concerns (auth/correlation), AddStandardResilienceHandler (.NET 8 — timeout/retry/circuit-breaker), the danger of retrying non-idempotent POSTs, and SocketsHttpHandler.PooledConnectionLifetime as an alternative. Middle creates HttpClient inside a using.
nodes.example_probe: Under load you get SocketException 'address already in use' even though HttpClient is in a using. Explain socket exhaustion and TIME_WAIT, why a static singleton isn't ideal either (DNS), how IHttpClientFactory solves this via handler pooling/HandlerLifetime, and which retry would make things worse on POST.

provenance.topic: Implement HTTP clients with HttpClient and IHttpClientFactory in ASP.NET Core Blazor

nodes.title: HttpContext, IHttpContextAccessor & Async Lifetime Pitfalls
nodes.description: HttpContext being bound to the request, the danger of capturing it in background tasks, the AsyncLocal mechanics of the accessor, response streaming, cancellation via RequestAborted.
nodes.senior_signal: Senior knows that HttpContext is not thread-safe and is valid only within the scope of the request — capturing it in a fire-and-forget Task leads to NREs/corruption (the context is reused/cleared). Understands that IHttpContextAccessor stores it in an AsyncLocal and the value is lost in Task.Run. Will talk about RequestAborted (client disconnected), response buffering, and streaming responses via IAsyncEnumerable. Middle passes IHttpContextAccessor around everywhere and uses Task.Run inside an action.
nodes.example_probe: In an action there is _ = Task.Run(() => ProcessAsync(httpContext.User)) and you intermittently get an NRE on User.Claims. What happens to HttpContext after the response, why won't IHttpContextAccessor inside Task.Run save you either (AsyncLocal), and how do you correctly offload the work (copy the data / IHostedService+Channel)?

nodes.title: DbContext Lifetime, Pooling & Thread-Safety
nodes.description: DbContext lifetime (scoped), thread-safety, DbContextPool, IDbContextFactory for Blazor/background work, state reset on return to the pool, and the incompatibility of pooling with scoped injection.
nodes.senior_signal: Senior will explain that DbContext is NOT thread-safe and why scoped breaks with parallel awaits on the same instance ('A second operation started on this context'). Will explain that AddDbContextPool reuses instances by resetting state, but does NOT reset custom fields/injected per-request dependencies → hidden sharing; that the pool is fixed-size and degrades under load; that pooling is incompatible with constructor injection of scoped dependencies. Will mention IDbContextFactory for Blazor Server and background work. Middle doesn't know why parallelism on a single context fails.
nodes.example_probe: Blazor Server with a long-lived component scope and parallel UI operations over a single DbContext — what errors will you get and how would you restructure it? How does DbContextPool differ from DbContextFactory, and when will the pool create a hidden state-related bug?

nodes.title: Change Tracking Internals & EntityState
nodes.description: Snapshot vs notification-based tracking, EntityState, the cost of DetectChanges on large graphs (O(n^2) in a loop), identity resolution, AutoDetectChangesEnabled.
nodes.senior_signal: Senior distinguishes snapshot change tracking (a copy of original values, O(n) per DetectChanges, O(n^2) in a loop) from notification entities (INotifyPropertyChanged). Will explain when DetectChanges is called implicitly (before SaveChanges, before a query, on access to Local/Entries), why AutoDetectChangesEnabled=false speeds up bulk edits and what it risks. Knows identity resolution (one PK → one instance) and its impact on no-tracking with duplicates. Middle doesn't understand the quadratic behavior.
nodes.example_probe: A loop of 50k updates in a single context runs quadratically slow. What happens inside the tracker on each iteration, and what two or three ways would you use to fix it without losing correctness?

nodes.title: Query Translation & Client Evaluation
nodes.description: Translation of LINQ to SQL, server- vs client-evaluation, why EF Core 3+ throws instead of silently doing client-eval, EF.Functions/HasDbFunction, pitfalls of untranslatable constructs.
nodes.senior_signal: Senior knows that since EF Core 3.0 untranslatable expressions in WHERE/ORDER BY throw InvalidOperationException instead of silently pulling the whole table (as in 2.x), and that client-eval is allowed only in the final projection. Will name the pitfalls: a C# method inside a predicate, DateTime.Now vs parameterization, StringComparison doesn't translate, .ToList()/AsEnumerable() in the middle of a chain kills server-side filtering. Knows EF.Functions (Like, Collate) and HasDbFunction. Middle can't tell where the code executes.
nodes.example_probe: Where will EF switch to client evaluation or throw and why — how do you rewrite it so a predicate with a helper method goes into SQL (expression/EF.Functions/HasDbFunction)? How does the behavior of EF Core 2.x differ from 8?

nodes.title: N+1, Loading Strategies, Split vs Single Query
nodes.description: Diagnosing/eliminating N+1 (lazy proxies, manual iteration, projection without Include), eager/lazy/explicit/projection, cartesian explosion with multiple collection Includes, AsSplitQuery and its consistency trade-off.
nodes.senior_signal: Senior distinguishes the causes of N+1 and diagnoses it via SQL logs/EventCounters. Will explain cartesian explosion with two collection Includes (duplication of root rows), projection into a DTO (Select) as a way to avoid unnecessary columns, lazy loading (virtual + UseLazyLoadingProxies) and its danger (a hidden synchronous round-trip inside async). Understands that AsSplitQuery eliminates duplication but issues N queries without a shared consistency point (risk of inconsistency — you need ORDER BY on a unique key, snapshot/serializable), and that split is not always faster (for small collections the round-trips cost more). Middle just says 'use Include'.
nodes.example_probe: An endpoint with orders + line items + payments: after Including both collections the payload grew several times even though there are few rows. What is happening at the SQL level, and which two EF mechanisms fix it with different trade-offs? When will AsSplitQuery make things worse, and at what isolation level will you get 'torn' data?

nodes.title: No-Tracking Queries & Projections
nodes.description: AsNoTracking vs AsNoTrackingWithIdentityResolution, projections into DTOs to minimize overfetch and bypass tracking, QueryTrackingBehavior.
nodes.senior_signal: Senior distinguishes AsNoTracking (faster, but duplicate instances on joins) and AsNoTrackingWithIdentityResolution (deduplicates at the cost of a dictionary). Knows QueryTrackingBehavior at the context level for read-heavy scenarios. Will explain that a projection into a DTO via Select doesn't materialize the entity, pulls only the needed columns, and doesn't load the tracker — often better than no-tracking over the full entity. Will mention that no-tracking does not disable identity resolution automatically. Middle slaps AsNoTracking on at random.
nodes.example_probe: A read-only API with self-intersecting navigations produces duplicates with AsNoTracking. Why, and which two options solve it with different CPU/memory costs? When is a projection into a DTO preferable to no-tracking over the whole entity?

nodes.title: Transactions, Optimistic Concurrency & Locking
nodes.description: SaveChanges as a unit-of-work, explicit BeginTransaction, optimistic concurrency control via rowversion/concurrency token, DbUpdateConcurrencyException, resolution strategies, pessimistic locking, isolation levels, lost update.
nodes.senior_signal: Senior will explain that a single SaveChanges is an atomic transaction and when an explicit BeginTransaction is needed. Will break down optimistic concurrency: [Timestamp]/rowversion vs IsConcurrencyToken, how EF adds the old value to the WHERE clause and throws DbUpdateConcurrencyException on 0 affected rows, resolution strategies (client-wins/store-wins/merge) via GetDatabaseValues/SetOriginalValue. Distinguishes optimistic (low contention) and pessimistic (SELECT FOR UPDATE, high contention) locking, the lost update/read-modify-write race, deadlocks and lock ordering, and that a concurrency token does not protect ExecuteUpdate/raw SQL. Middle does read-then-write with no protection.
nodes.example_probe: Two users edit a record and one silently overwrote the other. Optimistic vs pessimistic — which would you pick for a profile and which for decrementing warehouse stock, and why differently? What ends up in the SQL UPDATE, and how do you handle DbUpdateConcurrencyException for a merge (why are OriginalValues and GetDatabaseValues critical)?

nodes.title: SaveChanges Pipeline, Batching & Interceptors
nodes.description: SaveChanges internals: ordering by FK, command batching (MaxBatchSize), SaveChangesInterceptor vs override, audit/soft-delete via interceptor + global query filter.
nodes.senior_signal: Senior knows that SaveChanges batches INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE into a single round-trip (provider-specific, MaxBatchSize) and orders statements by FK dependencies. Distinguishes overriding SaveChanges vs SaveChangesInterceptor (reused with pooling, doesn't depend on inheritance) for audit fields, soft-delete (global query filter + interception), domain events. Understands that an async override must call the async base method and that ExecuteUpdate/Delete bypasses this pipeline. Middle doesn't know about interceptors and pooling.
nodes.example_probe: You need CreatedAt/UpdatedAt and soft-delete on all entities. Why is SaveChangesInterceptor preferable to an override when pooling is used, and how does soft-delete interact with global query filters? How does EF decide the order of INSERTs for a graph with FKs?

nodes.title: Bulk Operations: ExecuteUpdate/ExecuteDelete
nodes.description: Set-based bulk operations (EF Core 7+) versus per-entity SaveChanges, change tracker desynchronization, bypassing interceptors/audit/concurrency, lock escalation, batching.
nodes.senior_signal: Senior knows that ExecuteUpdate/Delete generate a single SQL statement without materialization and WITHOUT updating tracked instances (the tracker desynchronizes → stale data), and don't go through the SaveChanges pipeline (interceptors, audit, concurrency tokens, EF cascades don't fire — only database cascades do). Will compare with MaxBatchSize and bulk extensions for INSERT, knows about an explicit transaction when mixing the two, lock escalation with millions of rows, and batching by ranges. Middle writes a loop with SaveChanges.
nodes.example_probe: Update the status of 200k rows. Why is ExecuteUpdate better than a SaveChanges loop, and which three things will it silently bypass (audit, concurrency, tracking)? How does a bug arise if, after ExecuteUpdate, you access already-loaded entities in the same context, and how do you fix it?

nodes.title: Raw SQL, SqlQuery & Injection Safety
nodes.description: FromSql/FromSqlRaw/FromSqlInterpolated, SqlQuery<T> (EF Core 7/8), safe parameterization, composing LINQ on top of raw SQL, bypassing global query filters.
nodes.senior_signal: Senior distinguishes FromSqlInterpolated/FromSql (interpolation → parameters — safe) from FromSqlRaw (string passed as-is — injection risk, parameters only via DbParameter). Knows you cannot parameterize table/column names via value parameters, LINQ composition on top of FromSql (subquery), SqlQuery<T> for scalars/DTOs without a mapping, that raw SQL bypasses global query filters and concurrency, and that FromSql over an entity is still tracked. Middle concatenates strings.
nodes.example_probe: Where is the SQL injection hole, and why does FromSqlInterpolated close it while FromSqlRaw does not? Can you supply the column name to sort by via a parameter; if not — how do you do it safely? What does SqlQuery<T> return and how does it differ from FromSql over an entity?

nodes.title: Value Converters, Owned Types & JSON Columns
nodes.description: ValueConverter/ValueComparer (for mutable types), owned entity types (table-splitting), JSON columns (ToJson, EF 7/8), impact on queries/tracking/change detection, modeling value objects.
nodes.senior_signal: Senior knows why a ValueComparer is needed for mutable types under converters — otherwise change tracking does not see modifications (reference comparison). Distinguishes owned types (part of an aggregate, table-splitting) from navigations, and the limitations of owned types. Can explain JSON columns (ToJson): LINQ over JSON elements is translated into provider-specific SQL (OPENJSON/json_value), but indexing/performance are limited and the whole document is rewritten on change. Ties this to value objects in DDD. Middle does not know about ValueComparer.
nodes.example_probe: You store a List<string> via a ValueConverter into a column, and EF does not save changes to the list — why, and what do you need to add? When should you use an owned type, when a JSON column, when a separate table for a value object, and what are the performance limitations of queries over a JSON column?

nodes.title: Connection Resiliency & Execution Strategy
nodes.description: EnableRetryOnFailure/IExecutionStrategy for transient errors, interaction of retry with user-defined transactions (ExecuteAsync wrapper), idempotency, command timeout.
nodes.senior_signal: Senior knows that EnableRetryOnFailure enables an execution strategy that retries transient failures, but with an explicit transaction EF throws — you need strategy.ExecuteAsync(() => {...}) to retry the whole block, otherwise retrying half of it leads to inconsistency. Understands the risk of double-executing non-idempotent side effects and the importance of idempotency. Distinguishes transient from logical errors, configures maxRetryCount/maxDelay, knows command timeout is separate from retry. Middle turns on retry and does not think about transactions.
nodes.example_probe: You enabled EnableRetryOnFailure and wrapped two SaveChanges in BeginTransaction — why does EF fail, and how do you correctly retry a transactional block? Where would retry execute an operation twice, and how do you make it safe?

nodes.title: EF Migrations in Production
nodes.description: Idempotent SQL scripts vs Migrate-on-startup, migration race in multi-instance production, EnsureCreated vs Migrate, data migrations, __EFMigrationsHistory, drift. Related to the zero-downtime schema at the deployment level.
nodes.senior_signal: Senior does not run Migrate() on startup in multi-instance production (migration race, long-held locks), but generates idempotent scripts (migration bundle / script --idempotent) under CD/DBA control. Distinguishes schema migrations from data migrations and knows why a large backfill should not be pushed through a migration (locks, no batching/progress). Distinguishes EnsureCreated (no history, dev) from Migrate, knows model drift, __EFMigrationsHistory, the migration lock, and rollback as forward-fix. The depth of zero-downtime expand-contract belongs in deployment-rollout-migrations. Middle calls Migrate() on startup on every pod.
nodes.example_probe: 6 instances deploy simultaneously and each calls db.Database.Migrate() on startup — what goes wrong? Why is an idempotent script under CD safer, and how does EnsureCreated differ from Migrate?

nodes.title: async void & Fire-and-Forget Exception Handling
nodes.description: Why async void is dangerous, where it is acceptable, correctly launching background work without losing exceptions, unobserved exceptions, TaskScheduler.UnobservedTaskException.
nodes.senior_signal: Senior knows: an exception from async void goes to the SynchronizationContext and crashes the process, and cannot be caught by try/catch at the caller; async void is acceptable practically only in UI event handlers; a bare fire-and-forget (_ = SomeAsync()) loses exceptions and goes unobserved; the right approach is a wrapper with try/catch+logging, or a Channel/IHostedService; knows TaskScheduler.UnobservedTaskException and that in modern .NET an unobserved exception does NOT crash the process by default (unlike .NET 4.0), but that is no reason to lose it. Middle writes async void in handlers and _ =.
nodes.example_probe: In a controller, _ = SendEmailAsync(...) to avoid waiting. What happens to the exception if SMTP is unavailable, why can't you catch it in the controller, and why is background sending via async void in a timer even worse? How do you correctly do fire-and-forget with observability?

nodes.title: TaskCompletionSource & RunContinuationsAsynchronously
nodes.description: Bridging callback→Task via TCS, the main footgun — synchronous execution of continuations on the SetResult thread, deadlocks/priority inversion, SetResult vs TrySetResult.
nodes.senior_signal: Senior knows: by default the continuation runs SYNCHRONOUSLY on the thread that called SetResult/SetException — someone else's await code executes right inside your lock/callback → deadlocks, inversion, hijacking a library thread; the fix is TaskCreationOptions.RunContinuationsAsynchronously; distinguishes SetResult vs TrySetResult (a double-completion race throws InvalidOperationException), knows the non-generic TaskCompletionSource (.NET 5+). Middle calls SetResult without thinking about the thread.
nodes.example_probe: A wrapper over an event-based API via TCS, SetResult from a callback while holding its internal lock — rare deadlocks under load. Explain the mechanism and which exactly one flag at TCS creation eliminates it. How does SetResult differ from TrySetResult in a race?

nodes.title: Thread-pool Starvation
nodes.description: Pool exhaustion from blocking calls on async paths, slow hill-climbing growth, diagnostics via latency spikes, queue length and counters, distinguishing from GC pauses and lock contention.
nodes.senior_signal: Senior explains: the ThreadPool adds threads slowly (hill-climbing, ~1 per 0.5–1s above MinThreads), blocking on an async path consumes threads → cascading latency degradation; knows ThreadPool.SetMinThreads as a tactical hack and its downsides; looks at ThreadPool.ThreadCount/PendingWorkItemCount/dotnet-counters (System.Runtime), distinguishes starvation from GC pauses (gen2/pause %) and lock contention (Monitor Lock Contention Count); knows the dump with many threads in WaitOne and that the root cause (sync-over-async) must be removed, not the pool tuned. Middle says 'increase the number of threads'.
nodes.example_probe: A service under load shows p99 in seconds, CPU at 30%, GC is quiet, and it recovers after a minute. How would you prove in 10 minutes that this is thread-pool starvation, not lock contention or an external timeout? Which counters and what pattern do you expect?

nodes.title: Locking Primitives & Async-safe Mutual Exclusion
nodes.description: lock/Monitor, SemaphoreSlim (async WaitAsync), ReaderWriterLockSlim, System.Threading.Lock (.NET 9), why you cannot await under lock, reentrancy, lock convoy, contention.
nodes.senior_signal: Senior knows: you cannot await inside lock/Monitor (the lock is bound to a thread, the continuation may move to another); for async mutual exclusion you need SemaphoreSlim(1,1) with WaitAsync/Release in try/finally; knows reentrancy (lock is reentrant, SemaphoreSlim is not → self-deadlock), the new Lock (.NET 9) with EnterScope, when ReaderWriterLockSlim is justified, the cost of contention and lock convoy. Middle puts a lock on everything.
nodes.example_probe: Serialize access to a resource inside an async method (cache update, single writer). Why does a regular lock not compile / not work here, and what would you use? Show the SemaphoreSlim pattern. Where is the self-deadlock on a reentrant call, and what new does System.Threading.Lock bring in .NET 9?

nodes.title: CancellationToken Propagation & Linked Sources
nodes.description: End-to-end cancellation propagation, CreateLinkedTokenSource + mandatory Dispose, CancelAfter, cooperativeness, OperationCanceledException vs TaskCanceledException, registration leaks.
nodes.senior_signal: Senior talks about cooperativeness (the thread is not killed), CreateLinkedTokenSource and mandatory Dispose (otherwise a leak via the registration in a long-lived parent), the difference between OperationCanceledException vs TaskCanceledException (catch the former), ThrowIfCancellationRequested vs IsCancellationRequested, token.Register and the thread callbacks execute on, CancellationToken.None vs default, CancelAfter as a race-free timeout, and that cancellation does not guarantee an immediate stop. Middle accepts a token and sometimes passes it along.
nodes.example_probe: Limit an operation with an overall 5s timeout while respecting the external token from the HTTP request. Show the implementation. Where is the typical memory leak with a long-lived parent token, and how in a catch block do you distinguish cancellation-by-timeout from cancellation-by-client?

nodes.title: System.Threading.Channels & Backpressure
nodes.description: Producer/consumer on Channel<T>, bounded vs unbounded, BoundedChannelFullMode, backpressure for resilience, correct completion, comparison with Dataflow/BlockingCollection.
nodes.senior_signal: Senior chooses a bounded channel for backpressure, discusses BoundedChannelFullMode (Wait/DropOldest/DropWrite/DropNewest), SingleReader/SingleWriter, AllowSynchronousContinuations; correct completion via Writer.Complete(ex) and await foreach over ReadAllAsync; understands that an unbounded channel is a hidden OOM bomb when the producer is faster than the consumer; compares with TPL Dataflow and BlockingCollection (blocks a thread). Middle uses a ConcurrentQueue + loop, or unbounded.
nodes.example_probe: A stream of events from Kafka is processed by a pool of N workers, processing is slower than the inflow. Design a pipeline on Channels. What happens under a spike with unbounded, and which FullMode would you pick to neither lose data nor crash the process? How does backpressure from the bounded channel propagate back to the Kafka consumer?

nodes.title: Parallel.ForEachAsync & Degree of Parallelism
nodes.description: Data parallelism (Parallel/PLINQ, CPU-bound) vs async concurrency (I/O-bound), controlling the degree of parallelism, fighting unbounded fan-out, collecting all exceptions.
nodes.senior_signal: Senior distinguishes CPU-bound (Parallel.For/PLINQ) from I/O-bound (limited concurrency), applies Parallel.ForEachAsync with MaxDegreeOfParallelism or a SemaphoreSlim throttle; understands that Parallel.For blocks threads and is unsuitable for async bodies; that an unbounded Task.WhenAll(select) over 10000 items creates a spike on the DB/API and connection-pool exhaustion; knows how to collect ALL exceptions (WhenAll hides all but the first — you need task.Exception/AggregateException) and cancel the remainder. Middle does Task.WhenAll(select) on everything.
nodes.example_probe: Process 50000 URLs with HTTP requests as fast as possible without taking down the target service or the connection pool. Two approaches: SemaphoreSlim and Parallel.ForEachAsync. What is wrong with a naive Task.WhenAll(select)? How do you collect ALL exceptions and cancel the remainder on the first critical error?

nodes.title: PeriodicTimer, Timers & Long-running Background Work
nodes.description: PeriodicTimer vs System.Threading.Timer, tick reentrancy, async void in the callback, BackgroundService and reacting to stoppingToken, graceful shutdown.
nodes.senior_signal: Senior knows: the classic Timer invokes the callback on the thread pool and overlaps ticks if the work takes longer than the period (reentrancy), async void in the callback loses exceptions; PeriodicTimer.WaitForNextTickAsync gives non-overlapping ticks, cancellation, and no async void; understands that an unhandled exception in ExecuteAsync (.NET 6+) brings down the host (BackgroundServiceExceptionBehavior), the importance of reacting to stoppingToken and the ShutdownTimeout deadline, and drift between periods. Middle hangs a Timer with async void.
nodes.example_probe: A worker polls a queue every 10s, but one cycle sometimes takes 25s. Implementation with PeriodicTimer inside a BackgroundService. What would go wrong with System.Threading.Timer and async void given such variance? What happens to the host if an unhandled exception escapes ExecuteAsync, and how do you configure that?

nodes.title: Test Doubles, Isolation & Testability Design
nodes.description: Deliberate use of mock/stub/fake/spy, interaction vs state-based tests, fragility of over-specified tests, designing for testability without overengineering, a test double as a sign of a bad boundary.
nodes.senior_signal: Senior distinguishes stub (data) vs mock (verifiable expectation) vs fake (a working lightweight implementation, in-memory repo), talks about the fragility of interaction-based tests (mocks test the implementation, not the behavior), about fakes instead of mock chains, about when a test double is a sign of a bad abstraction boundary, about the danger of mocking types you do not control. Middle mocks everything and verifies calls via Verify (breaks on refactoring).
nodes.example_probe: A service makes 4 calls to dependencies, and the test verifies all 4 via Verify(). After a refactoring (same result), half of the tests went red. What is wrong with the design, and how do you rewrite it so refactoring does not break the tests? When is a mock justified, and when do you need a fake?

nodes.title: Deterministic Testing of Time & Async
nodes.description: Eliminating non-determinism: TimeProvider/FakeTimeProvider (.NET 8), testing timeouts/retries/debounce without real waiting, fighting flaky tests in async/multithreaded code.
nodes.senior_signal: A Senior knows TimeProvider/FakeTimeProvider (.NET 8) and why it is better than a hand-rolled IClock (it covers Timer, Task.Delay, PeriodicTimer, Stopwatch via GetTimestamp), advances virtual time via Advance() for retry/debounce, understands the sources of flakiness (races on ConfigureAwait, an uncontrolled SyncContext, reliance on timings, shared static state), and makes an async test deterministic via TaskCompletionSource/channels instead of polling. A Middle inserts Task.Delay/Thread.Sleep.
nodes.example_probe: Test a circuit breaker that opens for 30s after 5 failures and transitions to half-open, without actually waiting and without flakiness. How would you do it in .NET 8 with FakeTimeProvider? What does Advance() do with registered timers, and how does Polly v8 hook into TimeProvider?

nodes.title: Integration Testing with WebApplicationFactory & Testcontainers
nodes.description: The real pipeline (WebApplicationFactory) and real dependencies (Testcontainers) instead of in-memory, the unit/integration/e2e boundary, why EF InMemory does not catch SQL constraints, state isolation (Respawn/transaction/template), parallelism.
nodes.senior_signal: A Senior knows that InMemory does not catch SQL constraints/transactions/concurrency/raw SQL and is not recommended by the EF team, prefers Testcontainers with a real Postgres/SQL Server, replaces dependencies via WithWebHostBuilder/ConfigureTestServices, understands isolation between tests (Respawn/transactional rollback vs recreating the schema vs a template database), cost, parallelism with xUnit collection fixtures, and where to draw the pyramid boundary so as not to end up with an ice-cream cone. A Middle tests through InMemory and thinks they have covered the database.
nodes.example_probe: Tests via EF InMemory are green, but in production unique indexes and deadlocks blow up. Why does InMemory miss this and how would you restructure? How would you ensure data isolation between parallel tests against a single real database without drowning in container costs?

nodes.title: Structured Logging & Log Hygiene
nodes.description: ILogger with message templates, the LoggerMessage source generator, the IsEnabled check, scopes/correlation, the danger of PII/secrets, cardinality and the cost on the hot path.
nodes.senior_signal: A Senior uses message templates ({UserId}) for machine-parseable fields (not string interpolation, which loses structure), knows the LoggerMessage source generator (no boxing, no allocations before the level check, cached delegates), the IsEnabled check before formatting, log scopes/correlation id, the danger of logging PII/secrets (sanitization via [LogProperties]/redaction), cardinality and cost, and that high-volume logging on the hot path is a perf problem. A Middle writes LogInformation($"User {id}"), losing the structure.
nodes.example_probe: On the hot path (tens of thousands of RPS) logging has become a line item in the profile and in allocations. What is expensive in a plain LogInformation with interpolation (when is the string built even if Info is disabled?), and how do source-generated LoggerMessage and IsEnabled eliminate that?

nodes.title: Metrics, Histograms & Cardinality Control
nodes.description: System.Diagnostics.Metrics (Counter/UpDownCounter/Observable/Histogram), choosing the right instrument, percentiles vs average, cardinality explosion, bucket boundaries aligned with SLOs, RED/USE.
nodes.senior_signal: A Senior understands why the average latency is useless (you need histograms/p99), distinguishes counter/up-down-counter/observable gauge/histogram, is acutely aware of cardinality explosion (high-cardinality tags — ids, urls with parameters — blow up the TSDB, every combination = a separate time series), knows System.Diagnostics.Metrics vs prometheus-net, the built-in ASP.NET/HttpClient metrics (.NET 8), RED/USE and choosing bucket boundaries to match SLOs. A Middle measures the average and puts user_id into tags.
nodes.example_probe: After adding metrics, Prometheus eats memory and slows down. The code has a Counter with a request path tag containing an id (/orders/12345). Explain the mechanics (why the backend's memory grows) and how to rework it to use the route template. Why can't p99 be computed from a sum/count counter, and what is needed instead?

nodes.title: Distributed Tracing, OpenTelemetry, Activity & SLOs
nodes.description: Activity/ActivitySource as the native primitive, OTel as exporters on top, W3C traceparent propagation through HttpClient/messaging, tags vs baggage, sampling (head/tail/parent-based), linking traces with logs/metrics, SLI/SLO/error budget, context loss at async boundaries.
nodes.senior_signal: A Senior understands that Activity is the native .NET primitive (the OTel SDK is exporters/semantics on top), context propagation (W3C traceparent/tracestate) through HttpClient/messaging, the difference between tags and baggage (baggage travels over the network to all downstreams — it costs money/leaks data), sampling strategies (head vs tail-based, parent-based) and their trade-offs, linking trace_id with logs/metrics (exemplars), and where context gets lost (background tasks, custom pools, queues, ContinueWith without ExecutionContext). They think in terms of SLI/SLO/error budget and symptom-based alerting. A Middle turns tracing on with a checkbox and alerts on CPU.
nodes.example_probe: A request goes API→queue→consumer, and the trace chain breaks at the queue boundary. Why isn't the context propagated, and how do you pass traceparent through the message? How does baggage differ from tags, and why is it dangerous to stuff data into it? What sampling would you choose for 100k RPS, and why tail-based?

provenance.topic: Implement observability using OpenTelemetry and view data in Application Insights
Monitor and analyze metrics, logs, and traces

nodes.title: Resilience Patterns: Retry, Timeout, Circuit Breaker, Bulkhead
nodes.description: Polly v8 / Microsoft.Extensions.Resilience: retry with backoff+jitter, per-attempt vs overall timeout, circuit breaker, bulkhead/rate limiter, idempotency, the correct ordering of policies, ResiliencePipeline, retry storm.
nodes.senior_signal: A Senior knows that retries without jitter produce a retry storm/thundering herd, that only idempotent operations may be retried (and how to make a non-idempotent one idempotent via an idempotency key), the correct layering order (timeout inside retry = per-attempt vs outside = overall), why a circuit breaker is needed (fail fast, give the service room to recover) and bulkhead/rate limiter (pool isolation), Polly v8 ResiliencePipelineBuilder (not the legacy Policy.Wrap), and why retry+CB without backpressure make a cascade worse. A Middle slaps retry onto everything.
nodes.example_probe: A downstream degraded, your service finished it off with retries and then died itself from thread exhaustion. Walk through the chain: what made it worse, in what order should timeout/retry/circuit breaker go in the ResiliencePipeline, why jitter and bulkhead? Which operations must not be retried, and how do you make a POST safe to retry?
