nodes.title: Rate Limiting Middleware & Backpressure
nodes.description: System.Threading.RateLimiting / UseRateLimiter (.NET 7+): algorithms (fixed/sliding window, token bucket, concurrency), partitioning by key, QueueLimit, 429/Retry-After, in-memory vs distributed under horizontal scaling.
nodes.senior_signal: A Senior knows the differences between the algorithms (fixed window — a burst at the window boundary; sliding smooths it out; token bucket for bursts; concurrency for in-flight requests), PartitionedRateLimiter keyed by user/IP/API key, QueueLimit and OldestFirst, OnRejected with 429 and Retry-After. They understand that an in-memory limiter is not shared between instances (a distributed store is needed), that rate limiting by IP behind a proxy is meaningless without ForwardedHeaders, and that the limiter is backpressure complementing Kestrel's MaxConcurrentConnections. A Middle counts requests by hand in a dictionary.
nodes.example_probe: A limit of 100 req/min per API key with burst support and a queue of 10, returning 429 with Retry-After on rejection. Which algorithm and partition key, what is the catch with fixed window at the window boundary, and why will an in-memory limiter stop being correct when scaling out to 5 pods?

nodes.title: Health Checks & Graceful Shutdown
nodes.description: Liveness/readiness/startup probes for the orchestrator, SIGTERM draining of in-flight requests, cancellation via the host's CancellationToken, IHostApplicationLifetime, preventing loss of background work during deployment.
nodes.senior_signal: A Senior distinguishes liveness (is the process alive — restart) vs readiness (ready to accept traffic — removal from load balancing) vs startup probes, understands that readiness must not depend on external dependencies in such a way that a mild downstream degradation causes a fleet-wide restart, knows graceful shutdown: SIGTERM → stop accepting requests → drain in-flight within ShutdownTimeout, propagating the host's CancellationToken, IHostApplicationLifetime, and why a BackgroundService must respect the stoppingToken. A Middle serves a single /health=200.
nodes.example_probe: During a rolling deployment some requests get 5xx and background messages are lost. What happens on SIGTERM, how does readiness differ from liveness here, and how do you build a graceful shutdown so in-flight requests and background processing complete without losses? Why shouldn't you put the database into the liveness probe?

nodes.title: Secrets Management & OWASP for .NET
nodes.description: Protecting secrets (Key Vault, rotation, not in code/logs/git), mitigating OWASP classes in .NET: insecure deserialization (BinaryFormatter, TypeNameHandling), mass assignment, SSRF, injection, password hashing (PBKDF2/Argon2), constant-time comparison.
nodes.senior_signal: A Senior thinks beyond SQL injection: they know the danger of insecure deserialization (BinaryFormatter was removed from .NET 9 by design, TypeNameHandling.All in Newtonsoft = RCE, why System.Text.Json is safer — it does not materialize arbitrary types), mass assignment/over-posting (you need separate DTOs rather than binding into an entity), SSRF with user-supplied URLs, the difference between encryption and password hashing (PBKDF2/Argon2 with a salt, not SHA256), Key Vault + rotation + keeping secrets out of logs/git/appsettings, constant-time token comparison (timing attacks). A Middle only remembers SQL injection.
nodes.example_probe: In a code review: passwords hashed with SHA256, JSON with TypeNameHandling.All, an endpoint binding the request directly into an EF entity. Break down each one — what is the threat and what is the right approach. Why is BinaryFormatter insecure by design and removed, and how is System.Text.Json protected by default against the same class of attacks?

nodes.title: Production Profiling & Live Diagnostics
nodes.description: Live diagnostics without a restart: dotnet-counters/-trace/-dump/-gcdump, SOS (clrstack/dumpheap/gcroot/parallelstacks), distinguishing thread-pool starvation/deadlock/managed leak/LOH fragmentation, the overhead of observation.
nodes.senior_signal: A Senior captures live data without a restart: dotnet-counters for thread pool/GC/alloc rate/queue length, dotnet-trace for a CPU profile, dotnet-dump+SOS for hangs/leaks, gcdump for memory growth; they recognize starvation (growing queue length + low CPU, a symptom of sync-over-async), distinguish a managed leak (growing gen2/roots) from LOH fragmentation, and understand sampling vs allocation profiling and the overhead in production. A Middle adds logs and restarts the service.
nodes.example_probe: A service periodically stops responding, CPU is low, a restart helps temporarily, and restarting is not allowed — diagnose it live. With which tools and counters would you tell starvation apart from a deadlock and from a leak? What does the symptomatology of sync-over-async look like in dotnet-counters?

nodes.title: SOLID & Patterns Applied (vs Over-engineering)
nodes.description: Pragmatic application of SOLID and design patterns: spotting a violation, choosing a pattern that fits the problem, and — more importantly — not breeding abstractions where they are not needed (YAGNI, premature abstraction).
nodes.senior_signal: A Senior reasons in trade-offs: when DIP/an interface is genuinely needed (an unstable dependency, a module boundary, a second implementation) and when it is premature abstraction/speculative generality, spots LSP substitution violations and ISP violations in fat interfaces, distinguishes a pattern that solves a problem from a pattern for the pattern's sake, talks about cohesion/coupling and YAGNI, and can argue for removing an abstraction, not just adding one. A Middle quotes definitions and slaps an interface onto every class 'for testability'.
nodes.example_probe: A junior created an interface with a single implementation for every service 'so it can be mocked'. Where is that justified, where is it harmful, and how would you explain it in a code review? Give an example of an LSP violation that compiles and passes part of the tests yet breaks the contract.

nodes.title: Service Boundaries & Decomposition
nodes.description: Service boundaries drawn by business capabilities and data ownership (not technical layers), aggregate boundary = one transaction, bounded context, modular monolith vs microservices, the distributed monolith as an anti-pattern.
nodes.senior_signal: A Senior reasons about boundaries in terms of transactional consistency and data ownership: one aggregate boundary = one transaction; you cannot split what changes atomically. They will bring up bounded context, that a distributed transaction across services is an anti-pattern, data-on-the-inside vs outside, the danger of a shared database, and that premature decomposition (a distributed monolith) is worse than a monolith. They will cite the modular monolith as the default and the operational cost of each service. A Middle splits by technical layers or database entities.
nodes.example_probe: A payments monolith: accounts, limits, anti-fraud, notifications. Where are the service boundaries and why exactly there? What about the consistency of the debit and the limit check if they live in different services? What is a sign, already in production, that a boundary was drawn incorrectly?

nodes.title: Consistency Models & Distributed Transactions
nodes.description: Consistency models (strong/eventual/causal/read-your-writes/monotonic), why 2PC is impractical across services, database isolation levels, write skew, the inconsistency window.
nodes.senior_signal: A Senior operates with concrete models (strong/eventual/causal/read-your-own-writes/monotonic reads) rather than a dichotomy. Will explain why 2PC introduces blocking and a single point of failure at the coordinator → does not scale across services, whereas within a single database a transaction is appropriate. Will connect this to isolation levels (read committed by default, write skew, serializable/snapshot). Understands that eventual consistency is a convergence guarantee, not 'sometimes wrong forever', and quantifies the inconsistency window in numbers. A Middle treats a database transaction and distributed-system consistency as the same thing.
nodes.example_probe: Two concurrent requests debit the same account; the balance must not go negative. On a single database — which isolation level, and where is the write skew? If the account and the limit live in different services — why is 2PC bad and what would you offer instead of strong consistency?

provenance.topic: Set the appropriate consistency level for operations

nodes.title: CQRS & Read/Write Separation
nodes.description: Separating read/write models, materialized read models, eventual consistency on the read side, the read-your-own-writes problem, when CQRS is justified and when it is overengineering.
nodes.senior_signal: A Senior separates CQRS (two models) from Event Sourcing (they are orthogonal) and from physical database separation. Will explain that the read model is almost always eventually consistent relative to the write side, the lag in UX (read-your-own-writes) and the solutions (sticky read, versioning, reading from the write model after a command). Will name the costs: duplication, projections, rebuilding on schema changes, projection lag. Will say when CQRS is unnecessary (simple CRUD). A Middle considers CQRS mandatory or reduces it to 'separate DTOs'.
nodes.example_probe: Commands write to the primary database, a projection builds the read model. A user creates an order and immediately goes to 'my orders' — the order is not there. What is happening and what are the options to fix it without killing read scalability? How do you rebuild the read model on a schema change without stopping writes?

nodes.title: Concurrency Control & Locking (Architectural)
nodes.description: Optimistic vs pessimistic locking at the design level, choosing based on contention, lost update/read-modify-write, distributed locks and their unreliability (the Redlock debates), the connection to idempotency.
nodes.senior_signal: A Senior chooses based on contention: optimistic (rowversion/xmin/concurrency token, retry on conflict) under low contention, pessimistic (SELECT FOR UPDATE) under high contention with short transactions. Will name the lost update and read-modify-write race, deadlock/lock ordering, the danger of a long-running transaction holding a lock. Will connect this to idempotency and distributed locks (their unreliability — the Redlock debates). Keeps EF implementation details in ef-transactions-concurrency. A Middle does read-then-write with no protection.
nodes.example_probe: Two users edit a document; one silently overwrote the other. Optimistically and pessimistically — which one for editing a profile, which one for decrementing warehouse stock, and why differently? Why is a distributed lock via Redis unreliable?

nodes.title: Event-Driven Architecture & Messaging
nodes.description: Brokers (Kafka/RabbitMQ/Service Bus), event vs command vs document, at-least-once vs exactly-once, ordering (partitioning/session), consumer lag, queue vs log, DLQ/poison messages, competing consumers.
nodes.senior_signal: A Senior distinguishes event (a fact) vs command (a request) vs document message, understands at-least-once as the practical default, and exactly-once as an illusion without idempotency on the consumer. Will bring up ordering (partitioning by key in Kafka, single active consumer/session in Service Bus), consumer lag and backpressure, the difference between a queue and a log (RabbitMQ deletes after ack, Kafka keeps the offset and allows replay), DLQ/poison messages, competing consumers and why parallelism breaks ordering. A Middle 'just sends to the queue' with no guarantees.
nodes.example_probe: A publishes OrderPaid, B awards bonus points, the broker is at-least-once, B received it twice and awarded twice. How do you design B so this does not recur, and why would exactly-once-delivery not help? If there are many OrderUpdated events that must be applied in order — how do you ensure ordering without losing parallelism across different orders?

nodes.title: Idempotency & Deduplication
nodes.description: Idempotent operations/APIs: idempotency keys, deduplication on the consumer, atomic check-and-insert (UPSERT/unique constraint), handling repeats under retries and duplicates, the deduplication window.
nodes.senior_signal: A Senior builds idempotency as a property of the receiver: a unique business/idempotency key, a key store with TTL, atomic check-and-insert (UPSERT/unique constraint/INSERT ON CONFLICT) to eliminate the race between two parallel duplicates. Distinguishes natural idempotency (PUT/SET) from operations that require an explicit key (a payment). Will discuss the deduplication window, what to return on a repeat (the same response, not an error), the in-flight state (a second concurrent request waits/gets the same result), and the connection to the outbox. A Middle implements 'select then insert' with a race.
nodes.example_probe: A client calls POST /payments, gets a timeout and retries — but the first request went through. Design the API so the money is charged exactly once. What do you store, what key do you use, how do you protect against two simultaneous retries of the same key? What do you return on a repeat if the first one is still being processed?

nodes.title: Distributed Data Consistency: Saga & Outbox
nodes.description: Consistency across services without distributed transactions: Saga (orchestration/choreography), compensating actions, Transactional Outbox + CDC/poller for the dual-write problem, semantic locks.
nodes.senior_signal: A Senior solves this with a saga and compensations while being aware of the lack of isolation (intermediate states are visible, semantic locks/pending statuses are needed). Will explain the dual-write problem (a database write + publishing to a broker are not atomic) and why Transactional Outbox + CDC/poller solves it (the event is written in the same transaction, the relay delivers at-least-once → idempotency is needed on the consumer). Will compare orchestration (a central coordinator, visible flow) and choreography (coupling through events, hard to debug). Will note that a compensation is not a rollback and that non-compensable steps exist. A Middle proposes 'wrapping it in a transaction' across service boundaries.
nodes.example_probe: An order: reserve stock, charge money, create a delivery — without a distributed transaction. Design the saga: what happens if it fails at payment after the stock has been reserved? How does a service atomically save state AND publish an event? What about a step that cannot be compensated (the email has already been sent)?

nodes.title: Caching Strategies & Invalidation
nodes.description: Cache-aside/write-through/write-behind, distributed cache (Redis), invalidation and its races, cache stampede/thundering herd, negative caching, hot-key, in-memory vs distributed, HybridCache (.NET 9).
nodes.senior_signal: A Senior understands that invalidation is the hard part, discusses the cache-aside race (a reader stores a stale value between the database write and the key delete), why invalidate-on-write is preferable to update-on-write, and TTL as a safety net. Will name cache stampede on hot-key expiration and the solutions (single-flight/lock, probabilistic early expiration, stale-while-revalidate), negative caching, hot-key, the difference between in-memory and distributed (invalidation via pub/sub), IMemoryCache/IDistributedCache/HybridCache (.NET 9 stampede protection). A Middle implements 'GetOrSet with TTL' and considers the matter closed.
nodes.example_probe: A hot key with an exchange rate, TTL 60s, 10k rps. At the moment the TTL expires, what happens to the database and why? How do you prevent it? Separately: with cache-aside, which race leaves a stale value in the cache for a long time, and would HybridCache help?

nodes.title: API Design & Versioning
nodes.description: API contracts and versioning strategies, breaking vs non-breaking, tolerant reader, expand-and-contract, event versioning in the broker, schema registry, Asp.Versioning, System.Text.Json pitfalls.
nodes.senior_signal: A Senior thinks in terms of contract compatibility rather than 'let's add a v2': distinguishes breaking vs non-breaking (adding an optional field is safe; removal/type change/tightening validation is not), knows tolerant reader/Postel's law, expand-and-contract (parallel change). Will discuss event versioning in the broker (forward/backward compatibility, old consumers), schema registry, why URL versions breed forks, the different cost of breaking internal vs public APIs, Asp.Versioning, the danger of default serialization (enum, JsonIgnoreCondition). A Middle answers '/api/v2' and does not think about a rolling deploy with mixed versions.
nodes.example_probe: Rename a field in a JSON contract that is read by 5 services and mobile clients that cannot all be updated at once — with no downtime and without breaking old clients. What changes if it is a Kafka event that is stored and replayed? Why is adding a required field breaking even though 'I just added a field'?

nodes.title: Deployment, Rollout & Zero-downtime Schema Migrations
nodes.description: Blue-green/canary/rolling deploy, feature flags (deploy vs release), expand-and-contract database schema changes while old and new versions run simultaneously, the danger of destructive DDL on large tables.
nodes.senior_signal: A Senior designs deployment so that the old and new versions run simultaneously (rolling/canary), and derives migration rules from that: expand-and-contract (add nullable, write to both, backfill, switch reads, remove — never anything destructive in the same release as the code). Distinguishes deploy (the artifact) from release (the feature via feature flags), knows canary with metrics and rollback, blue-green and its database cost, the danger of long blocking DDL, idempotent/forward-only migrations. A Middle does a 'rename column' in a single step and takes down the old pods.
nodes.example_probe: Split the full_name column into first/last in a 200-million-row table, rolling deploy, traffic must not be dropped. Lay out the sequence of schema and code steps so that both versions work at every moment. Why can't you ALTER in a single release, and where does the feature flag fit?

nodes.title: Scaling, Partitioning & Sharding
nodes.description: Horizontal scaling, statelessness, sharding/partitioning, partition key selection, hot partition, cross-shard queries, read-replica vs sharding, global IDs (snowflake/ULID), consistent hashing.
nodes.senior_signal: A Senior distinguishes vertical/horizontal scaling and understands that everything bottlenecks on state (the database), not on the stateless application. Chooses the partition key (uniformity vs locality), sees hot partitions and cross-shard joins, discusses consistent hashing and rebalancing. Knows the difference between a read-replica (scales reads, replication lag) and sharding (scales writes), and that global IDs (snowflake/ULID instead of auto-increment) and distributed transactions become a problem after sharding. A Middle says 'add more instances/replicas' without analyzing the bottleneck and the key.
nodes.example_probe: The payments database cannot keep up with writes, replicas don't help, you shard. By which key do you shard the transactions table, and why that one? What breaks in reporting and ID uniqueness, how do you now generate IDs, and how do you implement 'all transactions for a period across all customers' after sharding?

nodes.title: Resilience, Backpressure & Graceful Degradation (System-level)
nodes.description: System-level resilience: cascading failure and its mechanics (thread/connection pool exhaustion), circuit breaker placement, a timeout at every level, bulkhead, load shedding, graceful degradation (stale cache instead of a 500).
nodes.senior_signal: A Senior designs for failure at the system level: knows that naive retries amplify an outage, applies backoff+jitter, a retry budget, and idempotency as a precondition. Will explain the exact mechanism of a cascading failure (what was exhausted — the thread/connection pool), circuit breaker (closed/open/half-open) and where to place it, bulkhead isolation of pools, a timeout at every level (its absence → pool exhaustion → cascade), backpressure and load shedding (better to refuse part of the load), graceful degradation (stale cache). Keeps the Polly implementation details in resilience-polly. A Middle adds 'retry 3 times' without backoff or timeouts.
nodes.example_probe: A calls B synchronously, B started responding in 30s instead of 50ms, and within a minute all of A is down even though B is alive. Explain the exact cascade mechanism (what was exhausted) and which techniques at which levels you would use to stop it. Why would retries make it worse, and where would you place the circuit breaker?

nodes.title: Observability as a Design Requirement & SLOs
nodes.description: Observability as a design requirement for distributed systems: what to log at saga boundaries, how to find a stuck message, correlation across the broker and async boundaries, the three pillars, SLI/SLO/error budget, symptom-based alerting.
nodes.senior_signal: A Senior distinguishes the three pillars (logs/metrics/traces) and understands that without correlation/trace context the path of a request through a distributed system cannot be debugged. Thinks of observability as a design requirement (what to log at saga boundaries, how to find a stuck message), not an add-on. Thinks in SLI/SLO/error budget, RED/USE, and distinguishes symptom-based alerting from noise. Keeps the OTel/Activity/propagation specifics in distributed-tracing-slo. A Middle 'adds some logs' without correlation and alerts on CPU.
nodes.example_probe: A customer says: 'the payment went through, the bonus points were not awarded'. The request passes through 4 services and a broker. How do you find within minutes where it got lost, and what must have been built in beforehand for that to be possible? Why are ordinary logs without correlation useless here?

nodes.title: Distributed AuthN/AuthZ & Service-to-Service Security
nodes.description: Authn/authz in distributed systems: token validation at the edge vs in each service, token propagation/on-behalf-of, service-to-service auth (mTLS/client credentials), stateless JWT vs reference token, revocation, defense in depth/zero trust.
nodes.senior_signal: A Senior understands where authn/authz lives in a distributed system: token validation at the edge (gateway) vs in each service, identity forwarding (token propagation, on-behalf-of), service-to-service auth (mTLS, client credentials). They will explain the trade-off of stateless JWT (cannot be revoked instantly → short TTL+refresh or introspection) vs reference token. They will name the dangers: trusting a token without verifying the signature/audience, authorization only at the gateway while the internal network is reachable (defense in depth/zero trust is needed), PII leaking into logs/traces. A Middle checks 'is the user logged in' at the entry point and trusts everything downstream.
nodes.example_probe: A request from a mobile client goes through the gateway into 3 services, one of which calls an external bank. Where are tokens validated, how does identity reach the 3rd service, and how does the 3rd service authenticate to the bank? The user must be logged out everywhere immediately — why is this non-trivial with JWT and what would you do?

nodes.title: Trade-off Reasoning & Capacity Under Load
nodes.description: Justifying decisions through explicit trade-offs, back-of-the-envelope calculations (throughput/latency/capacity/partitions), CAP/PACELC in practice, explicitly stating what is being sacrificed and where NOT to introduce complexity.
nodes.senior_signal: A Senior does not name the 'correct' pattern but exposes the trade-off and ties it to the requirements: CAP/PACELC in practice (what we sacrifice during a partition and what we sacrifice in its absence — latency vs consistency), the cost of strong vs eventual, sync vs async. Does back-of-the-envelope math: from tps and record size estimates QPS, data volume, number of partitions, p99, and sanity-checks the result. Explicitly states what they will NOT do and why (YAGNI, operational cost). A Middle presents a pattern as dogma, without numbers or trade-offs.
nodes.example_probe: A payment system at 10k tps peak, money must not be lost or duplicated, p99<200ms. Do a napkin estimate of the load on the database and the broker, justify where you need strong and where eventual consistency, and name what you deliberately sacrificed and in exchange for what. Where would you NOT introduce microservices/CQRS/event sourcing and why?

nodes.title: Micro-ORMs (Dapper) & EF-vs-Dapper Trade-offs
nodes.description: A deliberate choice of a micro-ORM (Dapper) instead of EF Core on hot read paths: manual management of connection/transaction lifecycle, mapping, protection against SQL injection in raw SQL, and justifying the EF vs Dapper trade-off.
nodes.senior_signal: A Senior justifies the choice of tool based on the workload, not out of habit: Dapper wins on read-heavy hot paths (no change tracking, identity map, query tree construction, or materialization into tracked entities — fewer allocations and less CPU), EF wins on domain logic with object graphs and a unit of work. They will explain manual ownership of the IDbConnection/transaction (opening/closing, the ADO.NET connection pool, an explicit transaction scope instead of SaveChanges), parameterization (Dapper caches and parameterizes — but string concatenation still opens the door to injection), multiple result sets (QueryMultiple), multi-mapping and splitOn, type mismatches, and buffering vs streaming (buffered:false). They will name the hybrid approach (EF for writes/domain, Dapper for reporting projections within the same transaction/connection) and the cost of maintaining two data-access stacks. A Middle drags one ORM everywhere and does not justify the choice.
nodes.example_probe: A reporting endpoint does 12 joins and returns 50k rows; the EF projection is bottlenecked on CPU and allocations during materialization. When and why would you switch to Dapper, and what exactly stops being spent? How would you share the connection/transaction between an EF write and a Dapper read within a single business scenario, and where is the injection risk here, given 'but I'm going through Dapper'?

nodes.title: GraphQL in .NET: DataLoader Batching, Query Cost & Schema Evolution
nodes.description: Senior-level aspects of GraphQL in .NET (HotChocolate): N+1 via DataLoader batching, limiting query depth/cost to protect against DoS, projecting resolvers into SQL, and evolving the schema without breaking clients.
nodes.senior_signal: A Senior centers the conversation on performance and security problems rather than on writing resolvers: N+1 in GraphQL is fundamentally worse than in REST (the client builds the selection graph itself) and is solved with DataLoader batching (a per-request cache, merging keys into a single query) and/or projecting resolvers into IQueryable. They will explain query depth/complexity/node limits and persisted queries as protection against DoS (a single deeply nested query brings down the database), cost analysis, and the difference between REST over-fetching and client-driven fetching. They will walk through schema evolution (adding a field is safe; removing a field or changing a type is breaking; @deprecated; nullability as a contract) and why versioning in GraphQL is done through schema evolution rather than /v2. They will compare GraphQL vs REST vs gRPC for a given scenario. A Middle writes resolvers and catches N+1 in production.
nodes.example_probe: A GraphQL query { orders { customer { orders { items } } } } hammers the database with hundreds of queries. Explain why DataLoader fixes this and how it differs from a plain cache, and why a projection resolver can eliminate the problem in a different way. How do you stop a client from taking down the service with a nested query of depth 20, and why doesn't ordinary rate limiting by HTTP request count help here?

nodes.title: gRPC: Contracts, Streaming & HTTP/2 Transport Semantics
nodes.description: gRPC for service-to-service: HTTP/2 multiplexing semantics, the four streaming modes, Protobuf contract evolution and backward compatibility, deadline/cancellation propagation, and the gRPC vs REST trade-off.
nodes.senior_signal: A Senior reasons about the transport and the contract rather than just calling the generated client: HTTP/2 multiplexing (many RPCs over a single connection, no head-of-line blocking at the request level, but it exists at the TCP level), the four modes (unary/server/client/bidi streaming) and when streaming is appropriate. They will explain Protobuf evolution: adding a field with a new number is safe, reusing or changing a number or type is breaking, reserved for removed fields, why there is no required, defaults instead of null. They will cover deadline propagation (the client sets a deadline, the server sees it and propagates it further, cancellation flows down the chain via CancellationToken), status codes vs HTTP, gRPC vs REST/JSON (binary contract, codegen, strict typing, but worse for browsers/public APIs → gRPC-Web/transcoding), and backpressure in a bidi stream. A Middle wires up the generated client and does not think about field-number versioning.
nodes.example_probe: Service A calls B over gRPC, B calls C, and the request has a 200ms budget. How do the deadline and cancellation reach C, and what happens to in-flight RPCs when it expires? In Protobuf you need to remove one field and add another — how do you do it so that old and new binaries coexist during a rolling deploy, and why is changing a field's number/type a silent breaking change?

nodes.title: SignalR & WebSockets: Scale-out, Backplane & Connection Lifetime
nodes.description: Real-time at scale with SignalR/WebSockets: scale-out with a backplane (Redis/Azure SignalR), connection lifetime and stickiness, backpressure on hubs, reconnect semantics, and message idempotency.
nodes.senior_signal: A Senior designs persistent connections across multiple instances, not a single hub: the fan-out problem under scale-out (the client is on instance 1, the broadcast is initiated on instance 2 → you need a Redis/Azure SignalR backplane or sticky sessions at negotiate), why the long-polling/SSE fallback requires affinity. They will explain the connection lifecycle (negotiate, transport upgrade, OnConnected/OnDisconnected, mapping user→connectionIds), backpressure (a slow client accumulates a buffer on the server → limits/eviction are needed), reconnect and undelivered messages (at-least-once on retransmission → idempotency/sequence numbers on the client, not 'just send it again'), and how many connections per instance memory/ports can sustain. A Middle adds a hub and tests on a single instance.
nodes.example_probe: A chat with 100k concurrent connections behind a load balancer across 10 instances. User A (instance 3) sends a message to a room where half of the participants are on other instances — how does delivery reach everyone and why is a backplane needed here? What happens during a brief network drop on the client side, and why does a naive 'resend on reconnect' produce duplicates?

nodes.title: API Gateway & Reverse Proxy (YARP/Ocelot) Patterns
nodes.description: Designing the edge boundary: routing and aggregation at the gateway, authentication offload, placing rate-limit/retry at the edge vs in the service (YARP/Ocelot/APIM), and managing contracts and access at the gateway level.
nodes.senior_signal: A Senior owns edge topology as an architectural decision, distinguishing it from in-process middleware: a gateway/reverse proxy (YARP, Ocelot, APIM) handles routing, aggregation (BFF), TLS termination, authn offload (token validated once at the edge) — but a Senior immediately adds defense in depth (inside the network you cannot trust the gateway alone). They will explain where to place cross-cutting concerns: rate limiting and coarse-grained retry belong at the edge, but retrying non-idempotent operations and business authorization do not; why aggregation at the gateway creates coupling and a single point of failure; versioning/deprecation and contract governance as a gateway function; the difference between gateway-per-client (BFF) and a single gateway. A Middle rarely owns edge topology and treats the gateway as 'just another middleware'.
nodes.example_probe: 10 internal services and a mobile/web client. What would you move to the gateway and what would you keep in the services, and why does authn at the edge not eliminate checks inside? Where would you place rate limiting and retry so as not to amplify a failure and not retry non-idempotent operations? What does an aggregating BFF gateway risk compared to a thin reverse proxy?
